### The joint
- Large head on a small socket → **most mobile and most dislocated** joint; **4 articulations** move together: SC, AC, GH (glenohumeral), scapulothoracic
  [[FIG: Fig 2.15 · 2.05
- Stabilisers
  - **Static** → glenoid + **labrum**, capsule and **GHLs** (glenohumeral ligaments), negative intra-articular pressure
  - **Dynamic** → **rotator cuff**, long head of biceps, deltoid, scapular muscles
- **Labrum** → fibrocartilage; deepens the glenoid ≈**50%**, gives ≈**20%** of stability (Prof Amr Rashwan)
  - Blood → from capsule and periosteum, **not** the bone; **anterosuperior** labrum poorest (Orthobullets)
  - **Long head of biceps** → anchored mainly to the **superior labrum**, not only the supraglenoid tubercle → why SLAP tears follow biceps traction (Prof. Maged Samy)
- Glenoid → covers only **¼ of the head**; width ≈**24 mm** (Prof Amr Rashwan)
  - **Scapular plane** = 30° in front of the coronal plane (Orthobullets)
  - Full abduction = 120° glenohumeral + 60° scapulothoracic, with **ER** (external rotation) to clear the greater tuberosity (Orthobullets)

### Stability — end range vs mid range
- Two ranges, two stabilisers (Prof. Amr Rashwan)
  [[FIG: Fig 2.16 · 2.05

| | End range (abduction + ER, >90°) | Mid range (45–75°) |
|---|---|---|
| Capsule | Tight | Lax |
| Main stabiliser | **Capsuloligamentous** (IGHL hammock) | **Negative intra-articular pressure** + **concavity compression** (cuff) |
| Defect that matters | Hill-Sachs | Glenoid defect |
